subtitle: Describe how Afghan Minnesotans arrived, the languages and peoples within the community, and how to offer respectful, well-matched service without guessing about any one person.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, eligibility and policy staff, communications and data staff, who want shared, accurate context before working with Afghan individuals, families and community partners.

lessons.title: From earlier arrivals to the evacuation: how Afghan Minnesota grew
objectives: Summarize the main periods of Afghan arrival to Minnesota using state refugee data.
Distinguish humanitarian parole, Special Immigrant Visa and refugee pathways at a basic level.
Explain why immigration status questions belong with the responsible program or legal service, not with general staff curiosity.
Identify one limit of state arrival data.
lessons.teaching:
Afghanistan has lived through more than four decades of war and upheaval: the Soviet invasion in the late nineteen-seventies, the civil war that followed, the first period of Taliban rule, the long U.S.-led military presence, and the Taliban's return to power. Each period pushed people out of the country. Minnesota Department of Health records show a small number of Afghan refugees arriving in Minnesota in the nineteen-eighties and a modest trickle over the next thirty years. Everything changed with the emergency evacuation that followed the Taliban's return.

In the months after the evacuation, Minnesota organized a rapid health response for newly arriving Afghans. A peer-reviewed account of that response counts about 1,260 Afghan evacuees in 386 families arriving in Minnesota in the first five months. DHS reports that Minnesota welcomed 1,363 evacuees during the first year. Arrivals continued afterward. In the most recent Minnesota Refugee Health Report, Afghanistan was the third-largest origin country for newly arriving people with humanitarian immigration statuses, with 603 arrivals, after Somalia and Ukraine. Hennepin County received the largest share, with Afghan families also living in Ramsey, Anoka, Olmsted and other counties.

Afghan Minnesotans arrived through several pathways. Many evacuees entered on humanitarian parole, which is temporary and gave access to only limited initial resettlement services. Special Immigrant Visas are for Afghans who worked for or on behalf of the U.S. government or the international security mission. Others came as refugees, asylum seekers, or relatives of people already here. Federal rules for these groups have changed several times, and an individual's status may have changed since arrival.

For DHS work, the practical point is restraint. Most staff do not need to know anyone's immigration status. Where a program's eligibility rules do require it, the eligibility process and the program's written guidance decide what to ask, and immigration legal services, not DHS staff, give advice about status. Keep in mind too that state arrival data count only people whose first U.S. destination was Minnesota. Families who moved here later from another state, or whose status has changed, may not appear in those numbers the way you expect.
lessons.keyPoint: Afghan Minnesota includes long-settled families and many people who arrived after the evacuation, through different and changing pathways. Leave status questions to the processes and legal services that need them.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Rahela, a DSD program specialist, is preparing an outreach plan for disability waiver information in Hennepin County. A colleague suggests adding a line to the sign-in sheet asking attendees whether they arrived on parole, a Special Immigrant Visa or as refugees, so the team can tailor materials. Rahela notices the outreach session does not determine eligibility for anything. She wonders whether the question will help anyone, and whether it may keep families away.
lessons.question: What should Rahela do about the proposed status question?
choices: Keep the question but make it optional, since optional questions cannot cause harm.
Drop the question and instead ask attendees which language and interpreter they prefer, directing any eligibility questions to the right intake process.
Replace it with a question about which province people came from, which is less sensitive.
feedback: Optional questions still signal what the agency wants to know. At an information session where status serves no purpose, the question can create fear and discourage attendance without improving the service.
This is the strongest choice. It collects only what improves the session, which is language access, and it routes eligibility questions to the process that has the rules and authority to ask them.

Province of origin can matter for interpreter matching, but collecting it on a sign-in sheet without a clear purpose is still unnecessary. Ask about language preference directly, and only when it helps the person.
lessons.reflection: Think about a form or intake step you use. Which questions on it are there because a rule requires them, and which are there out of habit?
lessons.action: Review one outreach or intake document you use this week. For each question that touches immigration or origin, write down the rule or purpose that requires it. Flag any question without a purpose and raise it with your supervisor or the program owner.

check.question: Why can state refugee arrival counts understate the size of an Afghan community in a Minnesota county?
check.correct: They count people whose first U.S. destination was Minnesota, so families who moved here later from another state may not be counted the same way.
wrong: They count only people who hold Special Immigrant Visas.
They include only people who have become U.S. citizens.
check.feedback: Minnesota Department of Health arrival data focus on primary arrivals, meaning people initially resettled in Minnesota. Secondary migration, family reunification and later moves mean the real community can look different from arrival tables. Treat the data as useful context, not a complete census.

lessons.title: Languages and peoples: Dari, Pashto and much more
objectives: Identify Dari and Pashto as Afghanistan's official languages and name other languages Afghans may speak.
Describe the ethnic diversity of Afghanistan, including Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek and other peoples, and the limits of population estimates.
Explain why a Farsi interpreter may not serve every Dari speaker well.
Plan an interpreter request that asks about language, dialect and comfort.
lessons.teaching:
Afghanistan's constitution names Dari and Pashto as official languages. Dari, a form of Persian, is widely used as a common language, and estimates suggest about half the population speaks it. Pashto is spoken by roughly a third. Other languages carry official status in regions where most people speak them, including Uzbek, Turkmen, Baluchi, Nuristani and Pamiri languages. Many people speak more than one language, and literacy in any of them varies with the schooling a person was able to get.

The country is also ethnically diverse. The largest groups are usually listed as Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara and Uzbek, followed by Turkmen, Baloch, Aimaq, Nuristani and others. Treat any percentages you see with care. Afghanistan has not held a full census since the late nineteen-seventies, and a later count deliberately left out ethnicity and language questions because they were so politically charged. Religion is similar: nearly all Afghans are Muslim, most Sunni, with a Shia minority that includes many Hazara. Small Sikh and Hindu communities also have Afghan roots. Ethnicity, region and faith have shaped who was targeted in past conflicts, so these are not neutral topics for everyone.

For language access, the details matter. The Minnesota Department of Health notes that Dari and Farsi are both forms of Persian, but a Dari speaker may or may not understand Farsi well, depending on where they are from. MDH also recommends orienting interpreters to a family's city or province of origin. Less common languages among recent arrivals include Hazaragi and Uzbek. So do not stop at asking whether someone speaks Persian. Ask what language the person prefers, whether a particular dialect matters, and whether they want written material or spoken explanation.

Comfort with a particular interpreter can matter too. A person may prefer an interpreter of a certain gender, or may worry about confidentiality in a small community. Ask these questions of everyone, in a neutral way, rather than assuming what someone wants from their ethnicity or appearance. The person's answer is the guide, not your prediction.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask for the person's preferred language and dialect instead of assuming Farsi, Dari or Pashto. Afghanistan's ethnic and language diversity is real, and estimates of it are uncertain.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Joel, a county case manager working with a DSD-funded program, schedules a Farsi interpreter for Marzia, an Afghan woman who is applying for services for her son. During the call, Marzia answers briefly and asks the interpreter to repeat several questions. Afterward the interpreter mentions that some of Marzia's words sounded like Hazaragi. Joel had not asked about language preference beyond the referral form, which said Persian.
lessons.question: What is Joel's best next step?
choices: Continue with Farsi interpreters, since Marzia did not complain and the referral form said Persian.
Ask Marzia's teenage son to interpret next time because he speaks English well.
Call Marzia with a Dari or Hazaragi interpreter, ask which language and interpreter she prefers, and note her answer in the file for future visits.
feedback: Short answers and repeated questions suggest a mismatch. People often do not complain about interpretation, especially early in a relationship with an agency. Waiting for a complaint puts the burden on the person.
Using a child to interpret for a parent in a service discussion about that same child raises accuracy, privacy and family role concerns. Use a qualified interpreter.
This is the strongest choice. It checks the fit directly with Marzia, uses a closer language match to ask the question, and records the preference so she does not have to repeat it.
lessons.reflection: When you request an interpreter, what do you usually know about the person's language beyond its general name? What would you need to ask to know more?
lessons.action: Look at the interpreter request process you use. Add or draft two prompts: one asking for preferred language and dialect, and one asking about any interpreter preference such as gender. Share the draft with your team lead.

check.question: Why should staff be cautious about precise percentages for Afghanistan's ethnic groups?
check.correct: Afghanistan has not held a full census in decades, and a later count left out ethnicity and language, so figures are estimates.
wrong: Because all Afghans belong to the same ethnic group.
Because the percentages have been fixed by treaty and cannot change.
check.feedback: Estimates are useful to show diversity, but they are not precise counts. Ethnicity and language have been politically sensitive, which is one reason formal counting has been avoided. Use the figures to remember that diversity exists, not to predict anyone's identity.

lessons.title: Family, gender and communication without stereotypes
objectives: Describe how extended family can shape decisions for many Afghan families while recognizing variation.
Distinguish offering choices about gender and privacy from assuming what a person wants.
Explain how name spelling and date differences can arise in records.
Draft neutral questions about who a person wants involved in a conversation.
lessons.teaching:
Many Afghan families place a high value on extended family. Decisions about health, money or a child's care may involve parents, spouses, older siblings or elders, and people may want relatives present at appointments. That is a pattern, not a rule. Afghan Minnesotans include people from cities and rural areas, people with university degrees and people who had little chance to attend school, people who worked closely with U.S. agencies and people who never did, and families who have lived here for decades alongside people who arrived in the past few years.

Gender is an area where stereotypes can do harm in two directions. Some Afghan women and men prefer a provider or interpreter of the same gender, especially for health or personal topics. Some want a spouse or relative present. Others do not. Many Afghan women were students, teachers, doctors, lawyers and public servants, and the restrictions placed on women's education and work after the Taliban's return affected them sharply. Do not assume a woman cannot speak for herself, and do not assume she wants a relative to speak for her. Offer the same choices to everyone: Who would you like in the room? Would you prefer a woman or a man as your interpreter? Then speak directly to the person, and when privacy matters, make sure they have a chance to talk without others present.

Faith practice varies as well. Many Afghans are observant Muslims and may fast during Ramadan, pray at set times, or prefer halal food, while others practice differently. Scheduling flexibility, such as avoiding meal-time meetings during Ramadan when asked, is a simple courtesy.

Records raise practical issues. Names written in Dari or Pashto script can be spelled several ways in English letters, and a family's members may not share one surname in the way English-language forms expect. Birth dates on documents are sometimes estimates. When records do not match, ask the person how their name should be written and which document to follow, and note variants rather than treating a mismatch as a problem with the person.
lessons.keyPoint: Offer choices about who is present, interpreter gender and privacy to everyone, then follow the person's answer. Family patterns are a starting point for a question, not a verdict.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Nadia, a DSD grants coordinator, is helping plan a listening session for Afghan parents of children with disabilities. A team member proposes holding separate sessions for mothers and fathers because that is what Afghan families would expect. Another team member worries that would exclude single parents and mothers who want to attend with their husbands. The community partner organization has not yet been asked.
lessons.question: What should Nadia do?
choices: Ask the community partner and a few parents what format would work, and consider offering both a mixed session and a women-only option.
Hold only separate sessions, since that is the cultural norm for Afghan families.
Hold only a mixed session, since separating by gender would be a stereotype.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It asks the people affected, uses the partner's knowledge, and offers options so different families can participate in the way that suits them.
Deciding for the whole community assumes one practice fits everyone. Some parents may prefer mixed sessions, and single parents may be left out.
Rejecting separate options can also exclude people, especially women who would speak more freely in a women-only space. Avoiding one stereotype by imposing another format does not solve the problem.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time a routine assumption about family roles shaped a meeting you were part of. What question would have tested that assumption?
lessons.action: Draft a short, neutral script for the start of your next meeting with a family: who they would like present, their interpreter preference, and whether they would like any part of the conversation to be private. Try it with any family, not only Afghan families.

check.question: Which approach best respects variation in gender and family preferences?
check.correct: Offer the same choices about who is present and interpreter gender to every person, then follow their answer.
wrong: Always direct questions to the oldest man present, since that is the family custom.
Never allow relatives to attend, so that every person speaks for themselves.
check.feedback: Both wrong answers apply one rule to everyone. Some people want relatives involved and some do not. Offering the same choices to all, and speaking directly to the person, respects both family ties and individual voice.

lessons.title: Service barriers and respectful practice
objectives: Identify common service barriers reported for Afghan newcomers in Minnesota.
Explain why staff should not ask people to retell evacuation or war experiences.
Distinguish information a service needs from information that is merely interesting.
Plan referrals to resettlement, legal and community resources.
lessons.teaching:
Afghan newcomers in Minnesota met several barriers at once. The account of the state's rapid health response describes an overstretched health system during the pandemic, a weakened resettlement network, and long uncertainty about whether parolees would qualify for federal benefits and health coverage. Those uncertainties have not disappeared for everyone. Some families still have relatives in Afghanistan or in third countries, may be waiting on applications, or face changing federal policy. Add housing costs, employment that does not match professional training, children adjusting to school, and grief for a country and a life left behind, and many people are carrying a heavy load when they contact a DHS program.

Many Afghans lived through violence, threats and a chaotic evacuation. That does not mean every person is traumatized, and it does not give staff permission to ask about it. Do not ask people to describe how they left Afghanistan, what they saw, or why they were at risk unless a specific, authorized process requires it and trained staff are doing it. Retelling can cause distress, and it rarely changes what a DHS program can offer. If a person chooses to share, listen, thank them, and focus on what they need now.

The same restraint applies to immigration status. Collect it only when a program rule requires it, and follow the program's instructions for what to ask. The Minnesota Government Data Practices Act governs how DHS classifies and protects the data it does collect; if you are unsure whether you may collect or share something, ask your data practices contact.

Respectful practice is mostly a set of good questions. What language would you like to use? Who would you like here with you? What is the most important thing we can help with today? Is there anything that would make this easier, such as a different time, a phone call or a woman interpreter? Know where to refer: the DHS Resettlement Programs Office and its Refugee and Immigrant Helpline, immigration legal service providers for status questions, and Afghan-led community organizations that offer interpretation, navigation and mental health support.
lessons.keyPoint: Meet present needs with good questions, clear referrals and care with data. Do not ask people to retell trauma or disclose immigration status that the service does not require.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Omar, a DHS call center specialist, takes a call from Fariba, who arrived with her family in recent years and is asking why her husband's health coverage letter says something different from hers. Omar's colleague suggests he ask how they came to the United States, what happened in Afghanistan, and whether they are still on parole, to better understand the family's situation.
lessons.question: What should Omar do?
choices: Ask about the evacuation first to build rapport and understand the family's background.
Confirm her language preference, look at what each notice actually says, explain it plainly, and refer status questions to immigration legal services and the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline.
Tell Fariba the difference is probably because of immigration status and suggest she contact a lawyer.
feedback: The evacuation story is not needed to explain a coverage notice and could be distressing. Rapport comes from being helpful and respectful, not from asking for personal history.
This is the strongest choice. It focuses on Fariba's question, uses the information that matters, and routes status questions to the people qualified to answer them.
Guessing the cause could be wrong and could alarm her. Look at the notices and explain what they say before suggesting anything else.
lessons.reflection: When a person's story is complex, what helps you stay focused on the question they brought to you?
lessons.action: Find and save the contact information for the DHS Resettlement Programs Office, the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline, and your division's data practices contact. Add them to a referral list you can reach quickly during calls or meetings.

check.question: When is it appropriate for general DHS staff to ask someone to describe what happened during their evacuation or flight?
check.correct: Generally never, unless a specific authorized process requires it and trained staff conduct it; otherwise focus on current needs.
wrong: Always, because understanding trauma helps staff build trust.
Whenever the person seems comfortable enough to talk.
check.feedback: Retelling traumatic events can cause harm and rarely changes what a DHS program can offer. Trust grows from respectful, useful help. If a person chooses to share, listen and return to what they need now.

cards.back: A temporary permission to be in the United States for urgent humanitarian reasons. Many Afghan evacuees first arrived this way; rules and later options have changed over time.
A visa pathway for Afghans who worked for or on behalf of the U.S. government or the international security mission, and their eligible family members.
Afghanistan's two official languages. Dari is a form of Persian; a Dari speaker may or may not understand a Farsi interpreter well.
In Minnesota refugee data, a person whose first U.S. destination was Minnesota. Counts exclude many people who moved here later.
Community context helps you ask better questions. It never tells you what an individual believes, wants or has experienced.

aid.heading: Before the conversation
items: Confirm preferred language and dialect, not only Persian or Afghan.
Ask whether the person has an interpreter preference, such as gender.
Check whether the task needs immigration status at all; if not, do not ask.
Allow extra time and offer a phone or in-person option.

aid.heading: During the conversation
items: Ask who the person would like present and speak directly to them.
Offer a private moment when personal topics come up.
Do not ask about the evacuation, war or reasons for leaving.
Confirm how names should be spelled and note variants in the record.

aid.heading: Referral and follow-up
items: Refer status questions to immigration legal services or the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline.
Connect to the DHS Resettlement Programs Office for resettlement services.
Offer Afghan-led community organizations as an option, not a requirement.
Record language and interpreter preferences so the person does not have to repeat them.
